Tenacious

tuh-NAY-shus -- stress on the second syllable, NAY. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Tenacious is determined and persistent; holding on firmly.

The tenacious weed pushed back up through the gravel no matter how many times it was pulled.

Worked Example

A junior reporter spends three weeks calling forty different sources, getting hung up on again and again, until the one person who saw the contract finally agrees to talk.

That refusal to let go of the story is tenacious: determined and persistent, gripping a goal the way a bulldog grips a rope. Tenacious people treat every 'no' as one step closer to 'yes.'

How Tenacious Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

persistent

persistent: continuing firmly despite difficulty

dogged

dogged: stubbornly persevering, refusing to quit

relentless

relentless: never letting up or easing off

Antonyms

irresolute

irresolute: wavering; unable to stay committed

yielding

yielding: giving way easily under pressure

How Strong Is It? — persistent → tenacious → relentless

persistent vs. tenacious

persistent vs. tenacious: Persistent is the everyday, milder word -- a persistent student keeps trying, while a tenacious one locks on like a vise and simply will not be pried loose from the goal.

relentless vs. tenacious

relentless vs. tenacious: Relentless pushes past even tenacious: a tenacious pursuit holds on through every setback, while a relentless one never pauses at all, allowing its target not a single moment of rest.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of tenacious.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — tenac-

Root — tenac-: holding fast (from Latin tenax, 'holding fast,' from tenere, 'to hold')

Suffix — -ious

Suffix — -ious: full of; possessing the qualities of (Latin -osus, via Old French -ous)

Put it together

Put it together: Tenacious is tenac- + -ious, the -ious variant of this unit's suffix family. Latin tenere means 'to hold,' and tenax means 'holding fast' -- so tenacious is literally 'full of hold': a grip, on a rope or a goal, that does not let go. You have already met this root in the noun tenacity, taught earlier in this course; tenacious is its adjective twin.

Use the root in a new word: retain

Use the root in a new word: retain: A well-built dam retains millions of gallons of water even through the heaviest floods.

Root Check

Word Choice

Tenacious is the adjective partner of the noun tenacity, which you learned earlier in this course: a tenacious climber shows tenacity. It also keeps its literal grip -- a tenacious vine, a tenacious stain -- anything that physically or figuratively holds on and will not let go.
